clue.text: Stocked by Manitoba store, revolutionary shoe

indicators.note: goods stocked by a shop sit inside it, so the answer lies within the run of letters that follows
a revolution turns something right round, so the concealed letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A Canadian shop in Manitoba stocks a radical new kind of footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a description of the shoe, but it tells you to read the concealed letters in reverse: TOBAS becomes SABOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabot is a wooden clog, traditionally worn by French and Flemish peasants.

clue.text: Ending in fisticuffs, a very bad argument in a Mayfair street

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written
vile means very bad
a row is a quarrel, rhyming with cow

explanation.surface: A nasty quarrel in a smart London street ends in a fistfight.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayfair is an expensive district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Savile Row is the Mayfair street famous for its bespoke tailors.

clue.text: Only taken in by foolish talk!

indicators.note: something taken in is held inside, so the first piece goes within the word that follows

blocks.note: alone means only, as in he alone knew
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that only a fool would be fooled by such nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' does double duty in the surface but here gives its own letters, split around the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Baloney is informal, chiefly American, slang for nonsense or humbug.

clue.text: Loftier spreading plant

indicators.note: spreading means sprawling apart, so the letters are scattered into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A taller plant that is spreading out.
explanation.definitionFit: Trefoil is any of several clover-like plants with three-part leaves.

clue.text: Listener baffled about one quick to bounce back

indicators.note: someone baffled is confused, so the letters of the word before are jumbled
about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A puzzled listener hears about someone who recovers quickly from setbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: LISTENER is rearranged as RESLIENT, and I is placed after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Resilient describes a person or material that recovers its shape or spirits rapidly after a blow.

clue.text: Stops rowing and relaxes

blocks.note: first meaning: literally, an oarsman pausing with blades out of the water
second meaning: the idiom for taking a break after effort

explanation.surface: A rower stops pulling and takes it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' might be read as quarrelling, but it is the boat sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to ease off after work, drawn from oarsmen leaning on their idle blades.

clue.text: Poorly in Devon, Keats, with me, treated in famous hospital

indicators.note: something treated has been worked on and processed, so the collected letters are rearranged

blocks.note: poorly means unwell
taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The poet Keats falls sick in Devon and is treated alongside the speaker at a well-known hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoke Mandeville in Buckinghamshire is a renowned spinal-injuries hospital, birthplace of the Paralympic movement.

clue.text: Terse, cheat in secular surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings enclose something, so the word for secular wraps the one for cheat

blocks.note: laic means lay, not clerical
to con is to swindle

explanation.surface: A curt summary: a fraudster operating in a non-religious setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Laic is a formal word for lay, meaning not belonging to the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech uses few words, like the famously brief Spartans of Laconia.

clue.text: Former partner, big enough for a model

blocks.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
ample means sufficient or large

explanation.surface: Someone's former partner is roomy enough to be a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a catwalk, but it means a pattern to copy.
explanation.definitionFit: An example is a pattern or specimen to be imitated, which is one sense of model.

clue.text: Drink rum in Torquay, empty

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its contents, leaving only its first and last letters
in places the first piece within the remaining shell

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the Devon resort
rum is old British slang for strange

explanation.surface: Drinking rum in a seaside town that has gone quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink, but it is the adjective meaning odd; 'Drink' at the start is the real definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot drink of spirits, sugar and water, often whisky.

clue.text: Appraisers in Virginia - new rules required

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters of the following word are reformed

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for the US state
the letters of rules rearranged

explanation.surface: Property assessors in Virginia must follow a fresh set of regulations.
explanation.definitionFit: Valuers estimate the worth of property or goods, which is what appraisers do.

clue.text: In which one may pick apples, or a variety of beet?

definitions.text: In which one may pick apples

blocks.note: taken as written
chard is a leafy vegetable of the beet family

explanation.surface: A question about where you go apple-picking, offering a vegetable as an odd alternative.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a synonym; 'or' is simply kept as it stands.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchard is a plot of fruit trees, the usual place where apples are harvested.

clue.text: Crayfish in sea - no glut, unfortunately

indicators.note: something that has gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fisherman laments that there is no surplus of crayfish in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Langouste is the French name for the spiny lobster, often called a crayfish or crawfish.

clue.text: Quick and inclined to bite?

blocks.note: first meaning: nimble, fast-moving
second meaning: apt to give little nips, like a snappy dog

explanation.surface: A description of a lively little dog that is fast and snappy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy is informal British for speedy, and literally describes something given to nipping.

clue.text: Descriptive of King James VI Golf Club in Scotland?

definitions.text: Descriptive of King James VI Golf Club in Scotland?

blocks.note: surface reading: words that fit a long-dead Scottish monarch, a king of long ago
setter's reading: the name of the famous golf club at St Andrews, which governed the rules of golf

explanation.walkthrough: A king is regal and James VI lived four centuries ago, so the two adjectives describe him; together they name the St Andrews club where he is said to have played.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews is the historic Scottish home of golf.

clue.text: Has Titian drawn islanders?

indicators.note: drawn suggests pulled out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A question asking whether the Venetian painter Titian sketched some Pacific islanders.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Gauguin, who did paint Tahitians; Titian lived long before.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahitians are natives of Tahiti, the largest island of French Polynesia.

clue.text: Revolutionary Muslim?

blocks.note: surface reading: a political radical or insurgent
setter's reading: a Sufi ascetic who literally revolves, spinning in a trance-like dance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests politics, but here it means turning round and round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mevlevi Sufi order is famous for its spinning devotional dance performed by these mystics.

clue.text: Welcomed in, strove to keep close to host

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the word for strove encloses the next piece
the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
vied means competed or strove
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A guest is welcomed in after striving to stay near the host.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welcomed in' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Welcomed' and 'in' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Invited means asked to come, a close synonym of welcomed in the sense of being received as a guest.

clue.text: Legendary German rock singer?

blocks.note: first meaning: a steep slate cliff on the Rhine famed in folklore
second meaning: the siren of legend whose song lured boatmen to wreck there

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock singer' suggests pop music, but the rock is a literal crag on the Rhine and the singer is the siren who sat on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the Rhine cliff and to the maiden of German folklore who sang from it.

clue.text: Phones circles at university

blocks.note: rings are circles
a student in residence is said to be up at university

explanation.surface: Someone telephones round student groups at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you go up to university and come down when you leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring up someone is the British phrasal verb for calling them on the telephone.

clue.text: Repeat? Learned start's missing

indicators.note: if the start is missing, the opening letter has been dropped from the word

blocks.note: literate means educated or learned

explanation.surface: A teacher demands a repeat because a learned piece's opening was skipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' looks like a past-tense verb, but it is the adjective meaning well-read; drop its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to do or say again, a formal synonym for repeating.

clue.text: Right and left, a rambler

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for right
left in the sense of remaining, as in food left over

explanation.surface: A walker who strays to the right and then to the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the opposite of right, but it means remaining.
explanation.definitionFit: A rover wanders from place to place, just as a rambler roams the countryside.

clue.text: Famous twin in rock band (American)

blocks.note: R.E.M. was an American rock band
abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: A well-known twin plays in an American rock group.
explanation.definitionFit: Remus and his brother Romulus were the legendary twins suckled by a wolf, founders of Rome.

clue.text: Smell around television at home in part of the Windward Islands

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the first word's letters wrap the pieces that follow

blocks.note: a scent is a smell
the usual abbreviation
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A smell hangs about a television in a Caribbean holiday home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At home' is the usual crossword way of saying in; the two short pieces go inside together.
explanation.definitionFit: St Vincent is the main island of St Vincent and the Grenadines, in the Windward chain of the Caribbean.

clue.text: Children's book laid out on rug

indicators.note: laid out suggests spread in a new arrangement, so the preceding letters are reordered

blocks.note: a mat is a small rug
the letters of laid rearranged

explanation.surface: A picture book spread out on the rug for children to read.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters are placed on, that is after, the rug.
explanation.definitionFit: Matilda is Roald Dahl's 1988 novel for young readers about a gifted girl.

clue.text: Finale of Maria Callas performing in opera house

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the last letter of the next word is used
performing suggests putting on a show, so these letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: the end of the first name
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The great soprano Maria Callas gives her last performance at a famous Milan venue.
explanation.definitionFit: La Scala in Milan is one of the world's most celebrated opera theatres, where Callas often sang.

clue.text: Diverting feature in fringe publication

blocks.note: the side of something is its edge or fringe
an issue is one edition of a magazine or paper

explanation.surface: An entertaining article appears in an alternative magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diverting' reads as amusing, but it means drawing attention away from the main point.
explanation.definitionFit: A side issue is a secondary matter that distracts from the central question.

clue.text: Iron in cupboard

blocks.note: first meaning: to smooth clothes flat
second meaning: a large storage cabinet, as for linen

explanation.surface: The iron is kept in the cupboard.
explanation.definitionFit: To press clothes is to iron them, and a press is also a tall cupboard for clothes or linen.
